title: The_Fable_of_Oscar
summary:
The Fable of Oscar is a fable proposed by John L. Pollock in his book How to Build a Person to defend the idea of token physicalism, agent materialism, and strong AI. It ultimately illustrates what is needed for an Artificial Intelligence to be built and why humans are just like intelligent machines.

In the fable, a race of Engineers who have all their physical needs provided by machines decides to create an intelligent machine called Oscar I. It has pain sensors and fight-or-flight responses to help it survive hostile environments. Oscar II is then built with a "pain sensor sensor" giving it rudimentary self-awareness; while Oscar I is like an amoeba responding to pain, Oscar II is like a worm that learns to avoid it.

Oscar III adds "introspective sensors," allowing it to sense the operation of its own sensors and form generalizations about their reliability, acquiring a higher degree of self-awareness. Oscar III can now determine if the environment is fooling it.

In the conclusion, Pollock considers a world populated by Oscarites. If sufficiently intelligent, they can philosophize about the difference between their outward physical state and inward mental state. While we describe them as sensing the operation of their perceptual sensors, they describe it as being self-aware and being conscious. Pollock states that while the Engineers are fictional, Oscar is real and we are in fact the Oscarites. Pollock later devoted considerable time to a software project called OSCAR, an artificial intelligence prototype he called an "artilect," which was largely an implementation of his ideas on defeasible reasoning as a LISP-based program with an interest-based reasoner.
